title: Wind chill only: no frostbite time is shown. That does not mean it is safe. The National Weather Service says exposed skin can freeze in 30 minutes or less at 0°F with a 15 mph wind (wind chill -19°F), and faster when colder or windier. Hypothermia is possible even above freezing.

c0.note: The constant term. NWS formula: Wind chill (°F) = 35.74 + 0.6215T - 35.75(V^0.16) + 0.4275T(V^0.16), T = air temperature (°F), V = wind speed (mph).

cT.note: Multiplies T. NWS formula: Wind chill (°F) = 35.74 + 0.6215T - 35.75(V^0.16) + 0.4275T(V^0.16), T = air temperature (°F), V = wind speed (mph).

cV.note: Multiplies V^0.16 and is subtracted. NWS formula: Wind chill (°F) = 35.74 + 0.6215T - 35.75(V^0.16) + 0.4275T(V^0.16), T = air temperature (°F), V = wind speed (mph).

cTV.note: Multiplies T times V^0.16. NWS formula: Wind chill (°F) = 35.74 + 0.6215T - 35.75(V^0.16) + 0.4275T(V^0.16), T = air temperature (°F), V = wind speed (mph).

exp.note: The power V is raised to. NWS formula: Wind chill (°F) = 35.74 + 0.6215T - 35.75(V^0.16) + 0.4275T(V^0.16), T = air temperature (°F), V = wind speed (mph). Defined only for air temperatures at or below 50°F and wind speeds above 3 mph; the chart covers 40°F to -45°F and 5 to 60 mph.

sources.name: National Weather Service, Wind Chill Chart
sources.used: the wind chill formula and its constants; 0°F with a 15 mph wind gives a wind chill of -19°F, at which exposed skin can freeze in 30 minutes; you might get hypothermia from cold when it is above freezing; wind speed at 5 feet (face height) from 33-foot readings; assumes no sun (clear night sky)
